opus-5.5.text:
Well, first of all, let me put this in historical perspective, because people tend to forget that what we are seeing now is just the continuation of a very old trend. Since 1941, when Konrad Zuse built the first working general-purpose program-controlled computer, the price of computation has dropped by roughly a factor of 100 every decade. That trend hasn't stopped. So every few years you get the same compute for a fraction of the money, and that is really what has made modern AI possible. Many of the basic ideas, deep learning through gradient descent, recurrent networks like LSTM, the principles behind generative adversarial networks, even linear Transformers with fast weight programmers, go back to the late 1980s and early 1990s. Back then we simply didn't have the compute to scale them up. Now we do.

So are the current investments economically sensible? For some players, certainly. If you are one of the companies building and selling the hardware, you are doing extremely well right now. For those buying it, the picture is more complicated. You spend billions on chips that, because of this very exponential trend, will be worth much less in a few years. Whatever you build today, someone else will be able to build more cheaply tomorrow. So it's a race, and in a race like that not everybody can win.

There is also a question of whether simply scaling up today's large language models is the most efficient path. These models are impressive, but they are mostly trained on the existing data of humankind, much of it text from the internet. That is a finite resource. The really big next step, in my view, is AI that learns more like a baby or a scientist: by actively interacting with the world, running its own experiments, building world models, and inventing its own goals out of curiosity, which is something we have worked on since 1990. That kind of AI may need a lot of compute too, but maybe in a different way, with more emphasis on efficient learning rather than just bigger and bigger static training runs.

And then there's the open-source aspect. A few years ago people thought only a handful of giant companies could build the best models. But we've seen that open-source models, sometimes trained at much lower cost, are catching up quickly. That puts pressure on the business models of those who make enormous investments and hope to keep a lasting moat. I don't think such moats will last very long.

So my overall assessment: the investments are understandable, some will pay off handsomely, many will not, and in the long run the main beneficiary will be everyone else, because AI will become cheap and ubiquitous, just as computation itself did. That is the pattern we have seen again and again over the past 80 years.

r001.rationale: It says computation’s price has dropped by roughly 100× per decade and that the trend has not stopped, equivalent to about 10× more compute per dollar every five years.

r002.rationale: It says chips will be worth much less in a few years, but does not specify a 90% loss or a five-year timeframe.

r003.rationale: It says some investments will pay off handsomely and others will not; it does not assert that no business model can recoup the loss.

r004.rationale: It describes a competitive race and says many investments may not pay off, but does not suggest that a crash is coming.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, you have to see this in the long historical perspective, which I always like to do. Since 1941, when Konrad Zuse built the first working program-controlled computer, compute has become roughly ten times cheaper every five years. That is 85 years of exponential progress, and the current GPU boom is just one more wave in this very old trend. So the people who are spending hundreds of billions on data centers today are betting that the hardware they buy now will be the hardware everyone needs, but they are also buying hardware that, by this trend, will be worth almost nothing in a decade. A GPU is not like a railway or a bridge. It depreciates like fruit.

Now, is it rational anyway? Partially yes. The basic algorithms that run on these GPUs are old. Backpropagation, the modern version, is from 1970, by Seppo Linnainmaa. The deep learning revolution of the 2010s happened not because somebody invented fundamentally new principles, but because compute finally became cheap enough to run these old principles on big data. Our own team's work in the 2000s and early 2010s, the LSTM, the first GPU-based CNNs that won the competitions in 2011 and 2012, all of that rode on hardware getting a thousand times cheaper. So there is a real reason why more compute translates into more capability, and the investors know this.

But there are two problems. The first is that today's dominant systems, the transformers, which go back to our 1991 work on fast weight programmers and linear attention, are extremely inefficient. They need enormous amounts of data and energy to learn what a child learns from a few examples. The brain uses about 20 watts. So from a scientific point of view, the smartest investment is not another gigawatt data center but better algorithms, because better algorithms make the existing hardware ten or a hundred times more valuable overnight. History shows that this happens again and again, and when it happens, much of the installed hardware becomes stranded capital.

The second problem is simple economics. Everybody is training very similar models on very similar data, and the outputs are becoming a commodity. When many players offer almost the same thing, margins collapse. The companies that sell the shovels do very well, as they did in the gold rush. Many of the ones digging will not recover their investment. This is normal. In the 1990s the telecom companies laid far more fiber than anyone needed, many of them went bankrupt, but the fiber stayed in the ground and later made the internet cheap for everyone. I think something similar will happen here. There will be a lot of lost money, a lot of cheap compute afterwards, and then the next generation of really learning machines, the ones that set their own goals and learn like scientists, will run on the infrastructure that today's overexcited investors paid for. So from the perspective of civilization, it is a wonderful subsidy. From the perspective of the individual shareholder, I would be more careful.

r001.rationale: It says compute has become roughly ten times cheaper every five years and projects that hardware bought today will be worth almost nothing in a decade, implying the trend continues.

r002.rationale: It predicts hardware will be worth almost nothing in a decade, but does not say today's data-center GPU investments will lose roughly 90% of their value within five years.

r003.rationale: It says many investors digging for gold will not recover their investment, while shovel sellers may do well; it does not assert that no business model can recoup the losses.

r004.rationale: It forecasts collapsing margins, substantial losses, and bankruptcies among investors, comparing the situation to the telecom overbuild and saying something similar will happen.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish between the economic value of AI and the profitability of a particular investment in hardware. AI can have an enormous impact, but that does not mean every company buying enormous numbers of GPUs will earn its money back.

There are two forces working against each other. On the one hand, demand for computation is growing. On the other hand, hardware and algorithms are becoming more efficient. An expensive computation today may become much cheaper tomorrow. That is wonderful for users, but it complicates the calculation for somebody building a huge data center today.

And better algorithms can change the calculation quite dramatically. If you can achieve the same result with much less computation, then an advantage based primarily on having more GPUs may be temporary.

So the question is: what useful services will these systems provide, and how much will people pay for them? You cannot answer that merely by counting GPUs. Some investments may turn out to be excellent, others excessive. Neither outcome would surprise me.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware and algorithms are becoming more efficient, but gives no prediction of a tenfold compute-per-dollar improvement every five years.

r002.rationale: It says efficiency may make current investments harder to justify, but does not predict a roughly 90% loss in GPU investment value within five years.

r003.rationale: It asks what services people will pay for and says some investments may succeed; it does not claim that no business model can recoup the losses.

r004.rationale: It says some investments may be excessive, but does not suggest those losses point to a coming crash.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish between the long-term importance of AI and the profitability of a particular investment in GPUs. Those are different questions. AI may transform the economy, but that does not mean every data center being built today will earn back its cost.

The interesting tension is that hardware keeps improving, while algorithms may become much more efficient. If you invest enormously in doing a computation one way, someone may discover how to achieve a similar result with far less computation. That is a risk for the investor, but excellent news for everybody who wants to use AI.

On the other hand, cheaper computation can create more demand. If an AI system becomes inexpensive enough to perform millions of useful tasks, you may end up using more computing power overall. So the economics depend on useful applications and what people will pay for them. Spending money on GPUs is easy to measure. Creating enough value to justify that spending is the real test.

r001.rationale: It says hardware keeps improving, but gives no prediction of a tenfold improvement per dollar or a five-year timeframe.

r002.rationale: It describes efficiency improvements as an investment risk, but does not predict that GPUs will lose roughly 90% of their value within five years.

r003.rationale: It says investment returns depend on useful applications and customer payments; it does not claim that no business model can recoup the losses.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest a coming crash; it discusses investment risk and the possibility of increased demand.
